 Stricter testing, lab reforms: TGA unveils tougher rules for sunscreen brands after SPF scandal
 Australia’s medicines regulator has revealed plans to rewrite the sunscreen testing rulebook after leading products fell short of their listed SPF ratings. 
 David Adams 
 Oct 27, 2026 
 2 min read 
 Share
 0 
 Prefer SmartCompany 
 Source: Adobe Stock 
 Australia’s medicines regulator has revealed plans to rewrite the sunscreen testing rulebook, a year after leading sunscreens fell short of their listed SPF ratings .
 The Therepeutic Goods Administration (TGA) on Tuesday proposed changes designed to bolster public faith after the shortfall scandal.

 TGA proposes sunscreen rulebook overhaul after bombshell reports
 David Adams 
 That scandal erupted after consumer advocates Choice independently tested 20 sunscreens and found 16 did not meet their sun protection promises.
 Among them was a sunscreen listed as SPF50+, which returned an actual SPF of only four. 
 As a result, a swathe of sunscreens were recalled from sale .

 On Tuesday, the TGA said the proposed changes are designed to “strengthen consumer confidence in sunscreen performance and ensure that sunscreen sponsors and manufacturers understand their regulatory obligations”.
 As it stands, sunscreen manufacturers do not need to hand their specific SPF testing data to the regulator when applying for a spot on the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG).
 This allows manufacturers to lean on SPF verification related to base formulas, before customising them in ways that could affect performance.
 After an initial industry consultation , the TGA now intends to change that rule, by asking manufacturers to provide SPF testing data on the finished product before official approval.
 Those brands would also need to hand over SPF data on a confidential basis, the ABC reports, prior to those final products landing on supermarket and chemist shelves.
 To prevent SPF performance from deteriorating over time, manufacturers would also need to test their packaged products at various points of their shelf life.
 Sunscreen testing methods could change too
 Related Article Block Placeholder 
 Article ID: 324223

 David Adams 
 Crucially, the way sunscreens are actually tested could change, too.
 Currently, businesses making sunscreen rely on in vivo testing, which sees sunscreens applied to human test subjects and SPF performance tested against infrared lights.
 Fearing SPF performance could vary between people with different skin types, the TGA wants to allow in vitro testing, where sunscreens are tested in isolation — and way from human skin.
 Additionally, the TGA said it is considering limiting the SPF claims of cosmetic sunscreens — which are skincare products with auxiliary UV-blocking benefits, on top of their core purpose. 
 Taken together, those reforms, if enacted, are likely to increase the testing and development costs borne by brands and manufacturers ahead of sale.
 Some changes could come into effect soon, while others would take more time to implement, given the need for extra consultation and potential changes to the law.
 The TGA is still mulling whether it should change the current SPF ratings system — which uses ratings like SPF15 or PF50+ — to a scale from ‘Low’ to ‘Very High’.
 “Further review and consultation on SPF labelling will be undertaken at a later stage before progressing with any proposed labelling changes,” said the TGA.
